faq-item.title: FAQ with structured data
faq-item.code:
<x-wirekit::faq label="Frequently asked questions" style="width: 34rem; max-width: 100%; margin-inline: auto;">
    <x-wirekit::faq-item question="How do I install WireKit?">
        Require the package with Composer, then include the style and script
        directives in your layout. No build step and no configuration file.
    </x-wirekit::faq-item>
    <x-wirekit::faq-item question="Is WireKit free to use commercially?">
        Yes. WireKit is MIT licensed, so you can use it in commercial products
        without a fee and without asking.
    </x-wirekit::faq-item>
    <x-wirekit::faq-item question="Do I need to write any JavaScript?">
        No. Every interactive component ships its own behavior, and you compose
        them from Blade like any other tag.
    </x-wirekit::faq-item>
</x-wirekit::faq>

faq-item.title: separated, md, and more than one answer open
faq-item.code:
<x-wirekit::faq variant="separated" size="md" multiple label="Billing questions" style="width: 34rem; max-width: 100%; margin-inline: auto;">
    <x-wirekit::faq-item question="When am I charged?">
        On the day you subscribe, and on the same day of each month after that.
    </x-wirekit::faq-item>
    <x-wirekit::faq-item question="Can I change plans mid-cycle?">
        Yes. The difference is prorated against the days left in the cycle, and
        the new plan takes effect immediately.
    </x-wirekit::faq-item>
</x-wirekit::faq>

reading-bookmark.title: Resume-reading pill triggered by a seeded prior visit
reading-bookmark.code:
Resume reading?

The pill in the bottom-right of this iframe is the resume-reading affordance. It surfaces when localStorage already holds a prior bookmark (saved on a previous visit, after the reader dwelled long enough and scrolled past the threshold). Click Resume to scroll the iframe to the saved position; click × to dismiss the pill while keeping the bookmark for the next visit.

This preview seeds a fake prior bookmark on mount via inline Alpine — the real component reads it back on init and shows the pill. On a real article you would not need the seed: the bookmark writes itself as the reader scrolls, and reads itself on the next visit.

The component clears the bookmark when the reader scrolls back to the top — at that point they are starting over, not resuming. It also reacts to cross-tab storage events, so dismissing the pill in one tab hides it in every other open tab on the same article.

Scroll inside this iframe to write a fresh bookmark on top of the seeded one (the seed updates with each scroll past the 10% threshold). Reload the iframe to see the pill reappear with the latest position.

Filler — keep scrolling

Cross-device sync is intentionally out of scope. The localStorage write is per-origin per-key; if you want a cross-device "resume on phone where I left off on desktop" experience, build a server-side bookmark via Eloquent (a column on the user-article pivot table) and listen for the same scroll events the primitive emits.

The pill is rendered with role="status" and aria-live="polite" — assistive technology announces the resume offer when it appears without interrupting the current reading flow.

The Resume button uses the accent fill; the dismiss button is icon-only with an aria-label. Both are keyboard-focusable and respect the same focus-ring tokens every other interactive WireKit primitive uses.

reading-meta.title: Time-to-read estimate above the article
reading-meta.code:
Estimating the read

The estimate is computed once on mount from the target's text, and the remaining figure follows the scroll position from there. Nothing is measured on the server: word count is a property of the rendered article, and the same markup delivered to two readers takes the same time to read.

Nodes that do not read at prose pace are skipped — code blocks, figures, captions, images and inline SVG. A page that is half listing and half prose would otherwise report a number nobody could reproduce by reading it, and an estimate a reader can disprove in ten seconds is worse than none.

Scroll this preview and the remaining figure comes down with it. The total stays where it started, because the article did not get shorter.

reading-minimap.title: Rendered mode — literal scaled-down preview
reading-minimap.code:
Rendered mode

Scroll inside this preview to see how the minimap paints an abstract content-texture map of the article body. Every paragraph, heading, code block, and image becomes a small colored rectangle on a canvas — the minimap convention of code editors, not a literal scaled-down clone.

The canvas is painted by walking every text-bearing node in the source via TreeWalker, getting per-rendered-line rects via Range.getClientRects(), and drawing each as a rectangle at minimap scale. Visual elements (img, figure, svg, video, canvas) are drawn in a second pass at their natural bounding box.

When to choose rendered over stripes

Pick rendered-mode when the visual rhythm of the page is part of the navigation cue — long-form articles with figures, code blocks, and varied section lengths. Pick the default stripe mode when raw density (one tick per item) reads clearer.

For very long articles (over 5 000 source DOM nodes) rendered-mode falls back automatically to stripes — the canvas-build pass is O(text nodes) and the budget keeps the cold-start cost bounded above that threshold.

Theme awareness

Each element type tints with its own color: h1 through h6 each get a distinct alpha tier (h1 darkest, h6 lightest); pre/code blocks tint indigo; tables tint rose; blockquotes tint slate-bolder; images tint amber; any [class*="wk-"] WireKit component tints emerald; prose and default tint slate-muted.

All 13 colors override via CSS custom properties on the minimap root (--reading-minimap-color-h1 through --reading-minimap-color-default). The component reads each token via getComputedStyle at paint time, so per-theme overrides apply automatically — no JS-side branching needed.

Performance characteristics

The minimap mounts lazily — the canvas isn't constructed until the wrapper enters the viewport. A MutationObserver on the source target rebuilds the canvas on meaningful content changes, debounced 250 ms.

Scroll tracking runs at one requestAnimationFrame tick per scroll event — compositor-only transforms, no layout thrash. Reduced-motion users get an instant snap-update instead of the rAF loop.

Keep scrolling — the more text you scroll past, the further down the minimap your viewport-overlay rectangle moves.

reading-minimap.title: Minimap stripes + viewport overlay tracking scroll
reading-minimap.code:
Overview

Each heading and paragraph in this article is rendered as a 1-2px stripe at the right edge of the iframe — that's the reading-minimap. Scroll inside this preview frame to watch the translucent viewport-overlay rectangle move down the column as the page scrolls.

The minimap sits at position: fixed against the iframe's viewport, so it stays pinned regardless of where the reader is in the article. Width defaults to 60px; the stripes inside are right-aligned and tinted with the accent token.

Stripe density

Stripe count equals the number of items the itemSelector picks up — by default 'a, h2, h3, [data-minimap-item]'. This preview overrides to 'h2, h3, p' so every paragraph renders as its own stripe; on a real article this gives a paragraph-level density overview.

Stripes thicker than 1px encode heading level (h2 thicker than h3, etc.). Paragraph stripes are 1px hairlines so the visual hierarchy survives at this scale.

Viewport overlay

The translucent rectangle on top of the stripe column tracks the host's visible region. Its top + height come from scrollY / scrollHeight and clientHeight / scrollHeight respectively, so the rectangle's vertical position + size always represent "where am I, and how much is in view".

Drag the rectangle to pan the host scroll position proportionally. Click any stripe to smooth-scroll the host so the matching item lands centered in the viewport.

Mobile behavior

The minimap defaults to hideBelow="lg" (hidden under 1024px viewport) because a stripe column at narrow widths competes with the article body for horizontal space. This preview overrides to "none" so the minimap is visible inside the iframe regardless of width.

For mobile-friendly density overviews, prefer the reading-spine — its collapsed-tick mode works at narrow widths.

Closing

The minimap is the densest of the reading-* primitives, but every primitive in the family follows the same contract: scroll-driven, IntersectionObserver-tracked, theme-aware via family-prefixed CSS variables.

Keep scrolling — the viewport overlay continues to move down as the article ends. By the bottom, the rectangle should sit at the lower portion of the stripe column.

reading-minimap.title: Heading anchors beside the minimap
reading-minimap.code:
Install the package

Require the package with Composer, then run the install command. It publishes the configuration file and tells you which step to take next, so a first run leaves nothing half set up.

The command is safe to run twice. It checks what is already in place and only adds what is missing.

Publish the configuration

The configuration file lists every option with its default and a short explanation. Change only what you need: anything you leave out keeps its default when the package updates.

Values that differ between environments belong in your environment file rather than in the published one, so a deploy never overwrites them.

Build your first page

Start from a layout component and fill its slots. A page needs a heading, a short introduction and one clear action. Everything else can come later.

Look at the page at phone width before you add more. Most layout problems are cheaper to notice with three components on the page than with thirty.

Choose a layout

A sidebar layout suits pages people return to and move around in. A centered column suits pages people read once from top to bottom, like this one.

Both collapse to a single column on a phone, so the choice is about how the page is used on a wide screen.

Add navigation

Link the sections of a long page from a table of contents, a spine or this minimap. The anchors beside the minimap are links like any other, so a keyboard reaches them and a screen reader announces them.

Keep the headings short. The anchor labels repeat them, and a long heading ends in an ellipsis once the label runs out of room.

Deploy

Build the assets, run the migrations and clear the caches, in that order. A deploy script that does all three keeps the steps from drifting apart between machines.

Keep scrolling: the viewport rectangle on the minimap follows you down the page, and the anchor for each section stays one click away.

reading-progress.title: Bar (default)
reading-progress.code:
Watch the bar fill as the page scrolls

The reading-progress bar pins to the very top of the iframe (its position: fixed anchors to the iframe's viewport, not the outer page). Scroll inside this preview frame — the bar's fill grows from 0% to 100% as the scroll position moves from 0 to the bottom.

The fill animation uses transform: scaleX — a compositor-only property, so the bar fills smoothly even on low-powered devices without triggering layout or paint. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce the transition collapses to 1ms; the value still updates on scroll, only the interpolation is removed.

Default height is 3px (height="md"). Pass height="sm" for a 2px hairline or height="lg" for a 5px chunky bar. The color is the accent token by default; pass intent="success" / intent="warning" / intent="danger" for semantic states.

The bar starts hidden until the reader has scrolled past showAfter pixels (default 0). Set a higher value (e.g. :showAfter="100") if you want the bar to appear only after the reader has committed to reading past the article header.

Pass :milestones="true" to fire wirekit:reading-progress:milestone events at 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%. Useful for analytics or for triggering a "you're halfway through" prompt where it makes sense.

The progress bar lives in its own DOM node and never interferes with the document flow — even when nested inside other components, it takes itself out of layout via position: fixed the moment it mounts.

If your page has a fixed header above the article, set position="bottom" to pin the bar to the viewport bottom instead. Both positions share the same Alpine state machine; only the rendered DOM differs.

For embedded contexts like browser extensions or iframes-within-iframes where the bar should match surrounding text color, pass intent="auto". The fill resolves to currentColor, so the bar inherits whatever color the surrounding context provides.

Keep scrolling — the more text you scroll past, the more visible the bar's fill becomes. By the end of this preview block the bar should be at or near 100%.

The progress bar is the lightest of the reading-* primitives — pure CSS plus a single rAF-throttled scroll listener. No IntersectionObserver, no localStorage, no DOM scanning of headings.

reading-progress.title: Dot indicator
reading-progress.code:
Watch the dot fill as the page scrolls

Scroll inside this preview frame and the dot's stroke fills clockwise as the scroll position progresses from 0 to the bottom. Same Alpine state machine as the bar variant; only the rendered DOM differs. The dot pins to the bottom-right of the iframe via position: fixed and renders as a circular SVG with a stroke that fills as the reader progresses.

The fill animation uses stroke-dasharray on the SVG circle — also a compositor-only property, GPU-accelerated. The dot doesn't take itself out of layout (it sits in its own fixed-position container), so it never interferes with the article flow below.

Use the dot variant when a horizontal bar would interfere with your layout — for example, if you already have a fixed top nav or a persistent CTA at the top. The dot is also less visually heavy than the bar; some product surfaces want the indicator to be discoverable but not prominent.

Hover the dot to see the percentage tooltip (the percentage is also exposed via the dot's aria-label for screen readers). On touch, the tooltip is suppressed; the percentage is still available via assistive tech.

Pass position="bottom-left" / position="top-left" / position="top-right" to relocate the dot. The default bottom-right follows the convention every messaging app and chat surface uses for "your status indicator".

The dot variant carries the same intent prop as the bar (primary, neutral, success, warning, danger, info, auto) — the color token threading is identical.

Both indicators (bar and dot) ship a @media print { display: none !important } rule via the .wk-reading-progress marker class. Print-friendly; the article body prints clean without progress chrome on every page.

If you need both indicators simultaneously (a bar for "where am I" plus a dot for ambient feedback), mount two <x-wirekit::reading-progress> tags side by side. Both share scroll state via the same plugin; neither knows about the other.

Keep scrolling to see the dot fill. The stroke completes as the reader hits the bottom of the article.

reading-progress.title: Reading-progress contained inside a card via boundary='container'
reading-progress.code:
{{-- 1. The contained reading surface establishes a positioning context (position: relative) AND a scrolling container (overflow-y: auto) with a defined height — both required for `position: sticky` to anchor correctly. Without these, the sticky strategy degrades to static and the bar disappears. --}}
{{-- 2. boundary="container" makes the bar use position: sticky and anchor to the nearest positioned ancestor — the wrapper above. --}}

Containment demo

Scroll inside THIS card and the bar fills as the local scroll progresses — it never escapes to the outer page viewport.

Each paragraph extends the scrollable area inside the card. Keep scrolling and the bar saturates.

A modal body, sidebar pane, preview frame, or Livewire panel are all valid container surfaces — anything with position: relative + a scroll-mechanism works.

Without boundary="container", the bar would pin to the OUTER viewport instead of this card, breaking the contained-reading metaphor.

More body text so the wrapper actually scrolls and you can see the fill react.

End of body.

reading-shell.title: reading-shell with defaults
reading-shell.code:
{{-- The CSS variable on the shell wrapper cascades to the inner spine so it renders narrow enough to fit alongside the article in this iframe; the article below reserves matching padding-right. --}}

Introduction

The shell renders a progress bar, a sidebar TOC, and a bookmark prompt with sensible defaults — drop your article body inside, pass a bookmark key, and the rest is opinionated defaults. The progress bar pins to the very top of this iframe; the spine sits at the right edge; the bookmark arms itself once you've dwelled long enough.

Scroll this preview to see all three primitives respond. The bar fills, the spine highlights the active heading, and after 30 seconds of dwell, the bookmark prompt appears bottom-right (only on a return visit — first visit shows nothing).

The shell wrapper is the 80% case: pass a bookmark key, accept the comfortable density default. For finer control, decompose into primitives and mount each one directly.

Body

Each primitive in the family carries its own Alpine state; nothing communicates between them. That makes the composition robust to changes in any one of them — opt out per-toggle (:spine="false") or pick a density preset (density="compact") without breaking the others.

The four primitives the shell composes by default: reading-progress (the bar), reading-spine (the sidebar TOC), reading-bookmark (the dwell-triggered prompt), reading-meta (time-to-read estimate, off by default). The minimap and TOC primitives are toggleable but disabled in the comfortable density preset — opt in via :minimap="true" / :toc="true".

The density preset (comfortable, compact, minimal) flips per-primitive defaults. compact uses a thinner progress bar and forces the spine to always-md expanded. minimal shows only the progress bar.

Conclusion

For per-primitive customization beyond what toggles + density cover, compose primitives directly. The shell covers the common case; dropping to primitives covers the rest, with no "shell-with-overrides" half-step in between.

The shell's div wrapper is the only structural element it adds. If your layout needs the article body to live inside a flex/grid container or a Livewire boundary, the shell's wrapper might interfere — that's the canonical signal to drop the shell and mount primitives directly.

Click any spine link to smooth-scroll to that heading. Click anywhere else to return reading. The bookmark saves your offset every second; on a real return visit (after 30s+ dwell time), it'll prompt you to resume.

reading-spine.title: Default spine
reading-spine.code:
{{-- The CSS-variable override narrows the expanded spine width so it fits the iframe gutter; the article below reserves matching padding-right. --}} {{-- .wk-reading-content reserves a responsive inline-end gutter for the fixed-position spine — full width below md (spine hidden), an 11rem gutter at md+ (matching this preview's 10rem expanded spine + 1rem offset via the --reading-content-spine-gutter override). --}}

Overview

The reading-spine is a fixed-position sidebar TOC at the right edge of the iframe. It auto-builds from the headings inside the nearest <article> or <main> ancestor, renders one tick per heading, and tracks the active section as you scroll.

Hover or focus the spine to expand the labels — collapsed it's just a thin column of ticks; expanded it shows full heading text. The expand-on-hover keeps horizontal space minimal until the reader actually wants to navigate.

Tick widths

Tick width encodes heading level: h2 ticks render wider than h3 ticks, which render wider than h4 ticks. This visual hierarchy survives at minified scale — the reader can tell nesting depth at a glance even before expanding.

Levels included default to levels="2,3" (h2 + h3). Pass levels="2" for h2-only (flat outline), or levels="2,3,4" for deeper hierarchies. The value is a plain comma-separated list — no inner quotes, which would be read as part of a level and cast to 0. Six levels (h1-h6) are valid; the plugin filters anything outside that range.

Active section detection

The active heading is the LAST heading whose top is at or above the offset line (default 96px), measured from the top of whatever scrolls — the page, or the region your shell scrolls in. This handles tall sections cleanly — a section longer than the viewport becomes "active" as the reader scrolls past its first paragraph rather than waiting for the next heading to enter the viewport.

Every scroll re-evaluates against live getBoundingClientRect(), at most once a frame, to find the currently-active item. A click holds its section until you scroll yourself, so the mark does not walk through every section the jump passes.

Smooth scroll on click

Click any tick → smooth-scroll to that heading. The URL hash updates via history.replaceState(), not pushState() — back-button still goes to the previous page rather than the previous heading. Saves the user from a multi-press back-button repro to escape the article.

Smooth scrolling is gated by prefers-reduced-motion: reduce — when the OS preference is set, the scroll happens instantly. Same gate applies to the active-state color transitions on the ticks.

Section-changed events

The spine dispatches wirekit:reading-spine:section-changed with details { index, id, text, level } when the active heading changes. Listen with x-on:wirekit:reading-spine:section-changed.window to update the browser tab title, fire analytics on section view, or sync state with a deeper component.

The dispatch is debounced 80ms — rapid scrolling doesn't fire 30 events for transient pass-throughs; only the heading the reader actually paused on triggers a callback.

Mobile behavior

The spine is hidden on viewports under md (768px) by default — hover doesn't exist on touch and the fixed sidebar would crowd a narrow viewport. Pass hideBelow="none" to show the spine even on mobile, useful for the collapsed-tick "I'm in section X" indicator without the expand interaction.

Filter slot: pass any input as the filter slot, two-way bind via x-model="filter". Items hide when their text doesn't match (case-insensitive substring). Useful for very long outlines (e.g. API reference pages with 40+ sections).

reading-toc.title: The reading family in one page
reading-toc.code:
Hero

Marketing landing page section one — a brief outline of what the page covers. The TOC strip pinned to the top of this iframe is sticky; scroll down and watch the active link follow you as each heading comes up to the strip.

The strip auto-scans <main> for <h2> elements (default levels="2") and renders one link per heading. No prop wiring required for the common case — drop the tag inside <main>, the rest is automatic.

Each link has aria-current="location" when active. The color comes from --reading-toc-color-active (the accent token by default). Idle state uses --reading-toc-color-idle (text-muted by default). Both transition over 150ms unless reduced-motion is set.

Features

The bullet-pointed pitch. Each feature gets a paragraph or two, all under the same h2. The active link flips as soon as this heading comes up to the line just below the strip, the same line a jump stands it on.

Click the "Hero" link in the strip to smooth-scroll back. The smooth-scroll math accounts for the strip's offset so the destination heading lands just below the strip, not under it. URL hash updates via replaceState — back-button still goes to the previous page, not to the previous anchor.

Per-link max-width truncation defaults to 24ch (--reading-toc-link-max-width). A long heading like "How to manage your team's billing settings" gets truncated to keep the strip from overflowing horizontally on narrow viewports.

Pricing

Three tiers, each with a card. Anchor links from the TOC strip jump straight to this section. The strip stays visible all the way down the page (it's position: sticky; top: 0 by default).

If your page has a fixed nav above the article, pass offset="4rem" on the strip to push the sticky position down by your nav's height. The same value moves the sticky position, the line a jump stands a heading on, and the line that decides the active section — three concerns, one offset value.

The list is wrapped in overflow-x-auto so a strip with 6+ items still scrolls cleanly without breaking the page layout. On mobile (under sm by default), the strip is hidden entirely — pass hideBelow="none" to show it on mobile if your design accommodates it.

FAQ

Accordion of common questions. Last anchor in the strip. The strip stays visible here too — the reader can jump back to any earlier section without scrolling all the way up.

For pages with more than 5-6 anchored sections, switch to the vertical reading-spine instead. The horizontal strip overflows fast at viewport widths under 1024px, even with per-link truncation. The spine's collapsed-tick mode is the right shape for dense vertical TOCs at narrow widths.

The two primitives (reading-toc and reading-spine) share the same data-collection model — both auto-build from headings via the same Alpine plugin pattern, both track the active section as the page scrolls. Only the rendered shape differs.
